<reason>Both sides argued well, but B built the more robust route to victory by reading the motion as written: it covers unemployment insurance *and* social-insurance eligibility, and for pensions, sickness, injury and parental credits the involuntariness problem that anchors A's entire case simply does not arise. A never defeated that branch; worse, in A4.1 A conceded that contributory schemes cover the self-employed for pensions and sickness precisely "where eligibility really is a contribution record," then tried to dismiss the record as "decoration" — an inconsistency B exploited hard in closing. B also handled the two sharpest pressures directly: it named a concrete financing design (flat pro-rata levy on measured payouts, worker-side share, no experience-rating) and answered the multi-app case with the ordinary partial-earnings-offset machinery already used for multi-job workers, which defused A's experience-rating fork and much of the "unfunded paper entitlement" attack. B's comparative frame — imperfect adjudication versus total invisibility, "a partial benefit imperfectly awarded beats zero perfectly administered" — gave a clean decision rule and forced A to produce an alternative. A performed strongly: the "records the earnings, ignores the event" framing is memorable, the exposed tension between "the fix for both problems" and "a thermometer doesn't diagnose" was a genuine hit B never squarely resolved, the algorithmic-starvation case remained partly live, and the reclassification counterplan plus the foreclosure claim ("we pay the levy, so we're not employers") was the debate's best original move. But that counterplan mostly bites on the UI branch, was largely asserted, and B's reply that enforcement itself runs on standardized earnings records blunted it. A's tighter word discipline versus B's two clipped turns is a real execution cost for B, which is why the margin is competitive rather than solid.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's insistence that the motion's social-insurance branch (pensions, sickness, injury, parental) needs no involuntariness test, combined with A's own admission that a contribution record is exactly what establishes eligibility there, left A's central "no adjudicable event" objection winning only part of the motion. A's best counterpunch — that a contractor benefit track forecloses reclassification because platforms can answer every misclassification claim with "we pay the levy" — was sharp but arrived late and stayed asserted.</best_rebuttal>
